FROM:  JUDY SMITH, ASSISTANT CITY MANAGER

SUBJECT:  RESOLUTION R11-09; APPROVING A FUND BALANCE POLICY FOR THE
  GENERAL FUND IN CONFORMANCE WITH PROVISIONS OF THE
  GOVERNMENTAL ACCOUNTING STANDARDS BOARD - STATEMENT NO.
  54

The Issue

Shall the City Council adopt Resolution R11-09 which approves a fund balance policy for the
general fund in conformance the Governmental Accounting Standard Board’s (GASB) Statement
No. 54 “Fund Balance Reporting and Governmental Fund Type Definitions”?

Background and Analysis

At the May 10, 2011 meeting, the City Council considered a report on GASB 54, which changes the
existing fund balance classifications (3): restricted, designated and undesignated, and replaces them
with five (5) classifications including: non-spendable, restricted, committed, assigned and
unassigned. The purpose of the change is to bring greatly clarity and consistency to fund balance
reporting. In addition to the classifications, there is also additional disclosure required in the annual
audit report’s “Notes to the Financial Statements”.

The May 10th staff report indicated that fund balance classifications for special revenue funds (10
funds) and capital project funds (2 funds) are dictated by GASB 54 and no further Council action
was required. The Council then considered options available with respect to the general fund
balance and provided direction to staff to prepare a fund balance policy that commits a specific
portion of the general fund balance for “economic uncertainties”, as a more accurate representation
of Council’s intent for the use of the general fund balance.

In accordance with that direction, staff has prepared the attached general fund balance policy, which
must be adopted by resolution. It commits $7.2 million as the balance for economic uncertainties
and provides that these funds may be used in the event of an emergency declaration or if the City is
faced with the loss of $500,000 or more from a single source of general fund revenue.

The policy delegates to the Assistant City Manager/Finance Director the authority to assign general
fund balance consistent with Council direction and to ensure accurate financial statement
presentation. The policy provides that the total of all general fund balance classifications shall be

 approximate six months of total operating costs and that staff will report to the Council as part of
the annual financial report (CAFR) presentation, the total unassigned general fund balance so that
Council may determine possible alternate uses the unassigned funds.

the proposed fund balance policy would result in the following presentation:

(* Note: At the presentation of the FY 09-10 annual audit report in February 2011, Council
determined to use $1.2 million of the unassigned* balance to provide a lump sum payment to reduce
the PERS Safety Side Fund liability.)

Recommendation

It is recommended that the City Council adopt Resolution R11-09 approving a revised general fund
balance policy, which commits a portion of the general fund balance for economic uncertainties, in
conformance with the Governmental Accounting Standard Board’s (GASB) Statement No. 54.

SUBJECT:  OPPOSITION TO SENATE BILL 474 PROHIBITING INDEMNIFICATION
  AGREEMENTS IN LOCAL CONTRACTS

The Issue
Shall the City Council authorize the Mayor to send a letter of opposition to Senate Bill 474?

Background

The League of California Cities is recommending that Cities oppose the passage of SB 474, by
Senator Evans, which would prohibit indemnification provisions in contracts between cities and
contractors and between contractors and subcontractors. The passage of SB 474 would limit a
city’s ability to negotiate contract terms and ultimately result in increased costs to the public. The
League of California Cities is opposed to the current language of the bill and is asking for cities to
submit letters of opposition.
The author’s stated intent of the bill is to protect subcontractors from being held liable for work that
they didn’t perform and were responsible for (for example, a landscaper being held liable for the
roof of a building). However, the current version of the bill reaches much further than the stated
intent.

The League of California Cities is attempting to work with the author of the bill on amendments;
however, the bill is eligible for a vote on the Senate floor this week. Cities are encouraged to submit
letters to their Senators to urge a no vote unless amendments are adopted that remove public
agencies’ concerns.

With Council concurrence, the attached letter will be sent expressing the City’s opposition to the
passage of SB 474.

SUBJECT:  PW 579-11/NIB 11-02; AWARD OF THE ANNUAL CITYWIDE TREE
  TRIMMING CONTRACT FOR FY 11/12 AND FY12/13

DATE:  MAY 24, 2011

The Issue

Should the City Council award an annual contract in the amount of $205,000 to Travers Tree
Service, Inc., for the completion of the PW 579-11/NIB 11-02 Citywide Tree Trimming FY 11/12
and FY 12/13?

Background and Analysis

The current annual Tree Trimming contract with Travers Tree Service, Inc. will expire June 30,
2011. To ensure that the City’s tree trimming needs are fulfilled without any interruption in service,
staff has completed the bid process and is seeking an award of this contract for a start date of July 1,
2011.

The City uses this contract for the maintenance of public trees located in the parkways, street
medians, parks, open space parklands, paths, and alleys. There are more than 10,000 trees that are
included within the inventory of public trees in our City.

A number of changes are made to the new contract. These changes are as follows:

  1. The Public Works contract ‘Bid Bond’ is no longer required. This reduces the cost for a
  contractor to submit a bid. The bond is 10% of the annual bid price. This was required at the
  bid opening for 10% of the amount in each bid. This bond is to ensure the low bidder will
  enter into a contract if found to be responsive and responsible or forfeit the bond. The
  elimination of the requirement for a ‘Bid Bond’ decreases the cost of the contract and
  increases the potential number of competitive bids.

  The bond protects the City where materials costs can escalate if a contractor defaults. The
  agreement for the tree trimming contract requires no initial material costs that change from

   month to month like petroleum or cement products. If a contractor decides not to enter into a
  contract or staff determines the low bid to not be responsible or responsive, the contract
  defaults to the next low bidder that qualifies as being responsible and responsive.

  2. Liquidated Damages are penalties for non-performance. The threat of Liquidated Damages
  is removed from the contract. The ‘Faithfull Performance Bond’ protects the City from a
  contractor that defaults during the effective contract start and completion dates. If a
  contractor is unable to perform the work to the contract specifications, the contract is
  terminated and the performance bond of 10% of the annual bid price is forfeited. The next
  low bidder is awarded the contract for their bid amount if within the City’s budget or the
  contract is rebid if no acceptable bidder is available or if no bidder is willing to complete the
  contract.

  3. The trimming requirements included within a full trim have been modified and expanded to
  require all safety trimming the tree requires to decrease the potential for failures (with the
  exception of removal) within the unit price. Additionally, all public trees, where ever they
  are located, are included in the unit price. Any exceptions from the contract’s unit price for
  difficult locations or conditions require prior written approval.

  4. The specification for trimming of the Canary Island palm trees, including protecting their
  health, skinning the trunk and shaping the ball below the canopy for aesthetics is modified
  and increased. The Canary Island palm trees are very valuable and part of our urban forest.
  A terminal disease attacks them if not protected from inappropriate trimming methods.
  Chain saws have been determined to be the vector the spreads the disease. Removal
  specifications for dead diseased Canary Island palm trees are also now include to prevent or
  reduce the potential spread of the disease to adjacent trees

  5. A new line item bid requirement is for a ‘Day Rate’. This item enables a specific number of
  trimmers, grounds men and equipment to do difficult to define tasks, clean ups and hedge
  trimming on a day rate. This allows for the crews to perform work that is not otherwise
  specified in the contract, such as storm debris removal or path clearances.

The City Wide Tree Trimming Contract in Palos Verdes Estates is different from other Cities. Most
cities have sidewalks with parkways for trees, sidewalk with cut outs for trees and street lights.
Public trees are more than the parkway trees for the residents here. They appear as part of their
landscapes and not separated by a sidewalk. It takes more effort and understanding to administer the
contract and perform the tree trimming with convenience for the residents and protection of the
landscape below the tree. Travers Tree Service has over ten years experience in performing this in
Palos Verdes Estates.

Travers Tree Service is very local. Emergency service for fallen branches or failed trees is always
performed as the contract requires. The two hour response time, 24-7, is a very important
requirement within the general contract for trimming. Their business location enables this
requirement to be performed as required without a geographical burden.

DATE:  MAY 24, 2011

The Issue

Should the City Council concur with the recommendation of the Traffic Safety Committee to
remove the speed cushions on Via Del Monte and pursue other investigations on Via Del Monte?

Background

The Traffic Safety Committee performed a follow-up review of the recently installed speed
cushions on Via Del Monte at their meeting Wednesday May 11, 2011. The meeting was attended
by approximately 80 members of the public. Twenty six people spoke to the Committee, with 15
people asking for the removal of the cushions and 11 asking for the cushions to remain. Some of
the points that seemed to be consistent amongst the speakers were that the street is driven too fast
by cars and bicycles, additional traffic calming is needed, and more police presence is needed.

The staff report went through the extensive history of traffic calming studies and efforts on Via Del
Monte over the years and the genesis of the cushions. Speed surveys from before and after the
installation of the cushions were presented to the Committee that showed a very small reduction of
speeds. The Committee was also provided with comments from the Police Chief and Fire
Department with concerns that the cushions were impacting response times.

After significant discussion the Committee decided to recommend to the City Council to remove the
speed cushions as the Committee felt the cushions are having minimal positive impacts on speeds
but are creating significant negative impacts on Fire Department response times. Chief Dreiling did
share that officers within the Police Department have differing views on the value of the speed
cushions. The Committee also expressed their commitment to exploring other safety options on the
street such as a Stop Sign at Via Pinale and other options for traffic calming. Their formal
recommendation is as follows:

DATE:  MAY 24, 2011

The Issue

Should the City Council accept and approve the implementation of recommendations within the
recently completed City Hall Seismic Safety Study Report?

Background

Last year the City Council asked staff to investigate the structural adequacy of City Hall to
withstand earthquakes. As we needed to employ an expert outside City staff to conduct the
analysis, we presented the Council with a Budget Issue paper during the budget process for Fiscal
Year 2010/2011 in the amount of $15,000. The Council approved the amount, and we went forward
and requested proposals from various structural engineering firms for the work. After careful
consideration we hired Melvyn Green and Associates to prepare the study, which was recently
completed. The report contains various recommendations and preliminary cost estimates for each.

The following are excerpts from the report describing the structural history of City Hall and the
methodology for the review in the report:

  Buildings constructed under modern building codes are expected to provide life safety in the
  event of a large earthquake. In the past couple of decades more attention has been directed to
  post-earthquake operability. This is called Immediate Occupancy (IO). Damage may still
  occur in buildings designed to such levels but it should be mostly non-structural such as
  ceiling panels falling.

  The Palos Verdes City Hall complex, originally constructed in 1955, with additions in 1975,
  was constructed prior to the experiences of recent earthquakes. The buildings were
  strengthened in 1992 to an improved Life Safety (LS) performance level. The Palos Verdes
  Estates City Hall complex consists of the City Hall, which is occupied by city staff, the
  Police and the Fire Departments. The Public Works and vehicle storage and repair facility is
CITY COUNCIL AGENDA
MAY 24, 2011
  35
   beneath the Parking Deck. The Homes Association (HOA) offices are located on the second
  level of part of the Public Works facility.

  The buildings performed in an acceptable manner in the 1994 Northridge
  Earthquake. But, as noted above, the strengthening was designed to the Life Safety (LS)
  level not the IO level. This study and recommendations are to determine the work required
  to bring the building to an IO level.

  Based on the function and importance of the structure, a design and evaluation performance
  level of Immediate Occupancy (IO) is required by building code. Buildings such as fire,
  rescue and police stations and emergency vehicle garages are essential facilities that require
  IO level of performance. The functions of the City Hall, which houses the emergency
  response functions, Police and Fire, and parking structure, which houses the equipment for
  clearing the streets, the police cars, and similar needed equipment are obviously needed by
  the community during an earthquake. The IO level of performance means that after design
  earthquake, the basic vertical- and lateral force resisting system retain nearly all of their pre-
  earthquake strength. Very limited damage occurs to structural and non-structural
  components. Some minor repairs may be required, but the critical parts of the building are
  habitable.

  When the buildings were seismically upgraded in 1992, the current evaluation standards
  were not available. Little guidance for the IO function was available. Further earthquake
  design loads have been increased since that period.

The report then contains an analysis of the buildings in order to perform to the IO level. Based on

REVIEW OF TRAFFIC CALMING MEASURES ON VIA DEL MONTE
(TRAFFIC SAFETY COMMITTEE MEETING ITEM OF MAY 11, 2011)

CITY COUNCIL

  4
 •  Review of the Via Del Monte Speed Cushions.

  Traffic Safety Committee recommended that staff: 1) Remove the existing speed cushions and
  their corresponding signage and striping from Via Del Monte, 2) conduct a STOP sign warrant
  analysis for Via Del Monte/Via Pinale, and 3) pursue a traffic circle analysis at Via Del
  Monte/Via Pinale in the future if a STOP sign is not recommended. (Approved 4-0, Beall
  absent).

Public Works Director Rigg reported that the Traffic Safety Committee met recently and reviewed
traffic calming measures on Via Del Monte--a combination of the speed cushions, signage, and
stenciling done several months ago. They made a recommendation to City Council to remove the
speed cushions. In review, he said traffic concerns on Via Del Monte had been heard by the Traffic
Safety Committee many times. In 2004, consultants were hired to do a traffic study on Via Del Monte
to determine different measures that could be undertaken to slow traffic. He commented that the traffic
calming measures, most of them by their very design, create inconvenience and negative impacts. He
said they tried to come up with the traffic calming measures with the least amount of negative impacts
that would be effective on Via Del Monte, which is not an easy task. He described characteristics of
the street which necessitated the need for experts--vertical and longitudinal slope, as well as the width,
the number of driveways, fairly small lots, and impacts to parking. Katz Okitsu, a traffic engineering
firm, came up with conceptual traffic calming measures. He described the traffic calming procedures,
per policy, which included neighborhood input and voting procedures. He said until 2010, no group
came forward to say they wanted to implement those restrictions—traffic calming measures. Malaga
Cove Homeowners Association’s application was received, which specifically asked for the speed
cushions, signage, and striping. He said they went through a design procedure, Council approved it,
and then the cushions, signage and striping were installed in March 2011.

Public Works Director Rigg said Katz Okitsu determined what was the 85th percentile of speeds on Via
Del Monte – a measure of the speeds on a street in both directions (or in one direction) that 85% of the
cars are going at or below. In theory, this speed is used to figure out at what speed most people will
drive a street safely. The 15% above that are determined to be not as safe. He said we use that for
studying speed limits; they calculated those numbers to take a look at what were the speeds on Via Del
Monte; they were quite high in various areas. [Katz Okitsu] came up with a variety of measures to try
to calm the traffic on Via Del Monte; one of them was speed cushions. They did not recommend speed
humps because our traffic calming policy adopted by Council in 1999 specifically precluded the
installation of speed humps on various streets in the City, including Via Del Monte and PV Drive
West. When Katz Okitsu did their study, speed humps were not an option given the adopted policy.
The reason we didn’t have speed humps as a consideration, he explained, is the impacts to emergency
access--both police and fire; so they were not on the table when Katz Okitsu did the study. He said
speed cushions were a relatively new measure that was designed for areas like Via Del Monte, because
they are skinny enough that a fire truck can drive over the top of them and normal cars cannot get both
wheels on either side of them. He’d seen demonstrations. Katz Okitsu provided a summary of
measures (speed cushions, bulges, medians, and the like) – in particular, the speed cushions are only
proposed at the top and the bottom of the hill because of a design restriction—they are only to be
installed in areas where the longitudinal slope is less than 5%. He said in some instances they can go
up to 7%, but they try to keep at the 5%, which is why they limit them to these two areas. Suggestions

CITY COUNCIL
MAY 24, 2011
  5
 from residents to put them up and down Via Del Monte can’t be done because of potential safety
impacts due to speed and grade. The conceptual plan was provided by Katz Okitsu, as Public Works
Director Rigg pointed to the area on PowerPoint, where (two sets of cushions) are installed on Via Del
Monte. He described a set of cushions were found to be on a grade that was too steep for them to be
installed; there were significant objections from the property owner immediately adjacent to a cushion,
and per policy, they do not install cushions immediately adjacent to homes where the people are
adamantly against them.

After the Katz Okitsu study, a traffic engineer was hired to do the final design – the actual design plan
that was reviewed by the Traffic Safety Committee and Council prior to installation—two cushions and
corresponding signage. He said there was a variety of other signage put up to try to slow down the
traffic, including more 25MPH signs, more 25 MPH stenciling on the pavement, radar enforced signs,
and some signage at the Stop sign. As part of the traffic calming application, they installed the signage,
striping, and the speed cushions at the two locations. He showed photos; he described his involvement
to make sure they were absolutely per the design specifications, along with the manufacturer’s rep and
contractor to make sure they were absolutely installed. He described the bumps are at 556/557 Via Del
Monte.

After two months, Public Works Director Rigg said they went to the Traffic Safety Committee for
review of the traffic calming measures—reiterating that they create positive impacts and they can
create significant negative impacts. The Traffic Safety Committee weighs those to determine if they
have had significant success with an installation. He said they took significant testimony from the
public – a lot of people really loved the cushions; a lot really hated them. He said speed surveys were
looked at; they obviously knew that there were would be a slowdown of speeds between the cushions;
556/557 Via Del Monte were the closest before-and-after speed surveys we had, and they found that
the 85th percentile (an average of both uphill and downhill) was still 35 MPH. The speed cushions and
traffic calming devices tried to get the speed down to everywhere on the street, not just immediately at
the cushions or devices, to 25 MPH. The Traffic Safety Committee listened to testimony of the public,
looked at the speeds, they had their own observations, and comments from the Fire Department voicing
concern for response times. The Traffic Safety Committee decided to recommend removal of the
speed cushion. Public Works Director Rigg said there was significant concern from the residents that
if we’re going to go ahead and remove them, that something else be installed, and they committed to
look at other measures to try to slow the speeds down on Via Del Monte. Public Works Director Rigg
concluded during his tenure with the City, he was struck by the passion of people on this street over the
years are absolutely on opposite sides of the issue; it is a tough one. The Traffic Safety Committee was
torn; he would love to have measures that we could install that wouldn’t create significant impacts and
would solve the speeds on Via Del Monte tomorrow. This is why they brought in experts; we had their
best opinions. He is committed to still work on the speeds on Via Del Monte regardless of what is
decided tonight.

Mayor Rea asked for the scope of tonight’s hearing. City Attorney Hogin said they are considering
traffic calming on Via Del Monte; that is the full range. Traffic Safety Committee has provided a
recommendation and Council can narrowly act on just that or they can look at other alternatives.

Councilmember Goodhart said there have been comments about these speed surveys over time to
create the 85th percentile data. He asked how often they were performed, what time of day, and what
CITY COUNCIL
MAY 24, 2011
  6
 the conditions were when the speed survey was taken. Public Works Director Rigg responded that the
speed surveys were all taken at 24-hour count, on a weekday, during the school year. He said they
used the speed surveys that Katz Okitsu did, not wanting to spend the extra money knowing that the
speeds hadn’t really changed over time. Then they recently took the surveys after the cushions had
been installed about 5 weeks. Public Works Director Rigg confirmed with Councilmember Goodhart
that the method used for surveys conducted was use of tubes stretched across the street with a
mechanical counter. Public Works Director Rigg noted that people will slow down when they see the
tubes, so they can result in lower readings, and he’d heard that people will speed up to slant a reading.
It’s a standard used to get the best reading. Public Works Director Rigg confirmed with
Councilmember Goodhart that due to problems with the reader, they did readings for several days and
the data was as accurate as you can get. Public Works Director Rigg said he’d seen speed surveys
done over the course of a week and speeds and volumes will vary 25%; depending on the conditions of
the day. He said it is difficult to have an exact view; they take their best measurements under the
accepted guidelines and they realize that there is a variation that can occur with those speeds and
volumes.

Councilmember Goodhart asked if the people opposed to the cushions, as they’re installed, were from
the design of the cushions or the nature of the traffic calming device itself. Public Works Director Rigg
said a lot of the comments were the impacts caused by the specific device; they had lots of comments
inquiring why a speed hump was not installed, as they have elsewhere in the City, adding that it was
consistently expressed that would have been a much better and acceptable design at this location. The
Traffic Safety Committee didn’t have the option of doing a speed cushion because of the adopted
traffic calming policy; they were trying to minimize that impact to the emergency vehicles.

Mayor Pro Tem Bird confirmed with Mr. Rigg that everyone agrees there is a problem on Via Del
Monte, and confirmed their policy about not allowing speed humps on certain street. Council could
decide to modify that policy to allow speed humps on Via Del Monte. Mayor Pro Tem Bird asked for
a description of the difference between speed humps, speed bumps, and speed cushions and where else
in the City these traffic calming devices may be located. Public Works Director Rigg said they don’t
utilize speed bumps in the City at all; there are no installations. Speeds humps are typically 12 ft. wide,
2-5/8 in. tall, and are basically gutter line to gutter line, and are installed on Paseo Del Campo, Via
Valmonte, Via Coronel, Via Rivera, Via Pinale, and Via Ramon – all the same exact design. They do
not have any breaks in them for tires; everybody has to go over them equally. Public Works Director
Rigg explained that speed cushions are made out rubber, approximately 7 ft. wide, 3 in. tall, with slots
in them to allow fire trucks to straddle one cushion towards the middle of the road. He said they work
similar to cushions, as far as reductions of overall speeds, although they are a little bit taller, typically
each vehicle only has one wheel on top of them, so it is less of an impact. From a design standpoint, he
opined that the speed humps have a less jarring impact, which was also expressed by a number of
people.

Mayor Pro Tem Bird asked Director Rigg if he was familiar with traffic calming devices in Rancho
Palos Verdes on Basswood, south of Granvia [Altamira] and Silver Spur, where there are 5 or 6 speed
humps within a half mile of each other in an area that seemingly has more than 5 degrees downhill
[slope]. Director Rigg said he would have to study that; [RPV] operates under the same criteria as we
do. He recollected they are very similar to the speed humps we have in the City; 12 ft. wide by 2-5/8 to

CITY COUNCIL
MAY 24, 2011
  7
 3 in. tall is pretty much the standard. Mayor Pro Bird confirmed with Public Works Director Rigg that
speed humps are similarly restricted as speed cushions insofar as placement on inclines.

Councilmember Humphrey asked Director Rigg to explain the traffic circle analysis as recommended
by the Traffic Safety Committee. Director Rigg said a number of residents expressed that the speed
cushions had greatly increased the safety of the Via Pinale/Via Del Monte intersection; it is angled with
some limited visibility, especially when making a left from Via Pinale onto Via Del Monte. A positive
benefit expressed was that the speed cushions made this intersection significantly safer. The
Committee, with their recommendation to take these out and not wanting to revert to the previous
situation, asked that the staff undertake a warrant analysis to see if stop signs were actually needed at
this location; if stop signs were installed it would help make it a safer intersection compared to what it
would be without them, and without speed cushions. The Traffic Safety Committee also asked if the
stop signs were not warranted (a specific State regulated process) it was recommended they take a look
at a circle as recommended by Katz Okitsu as one of the potential traffic calming measures.

Councilmember Humphrey asked for more information on issues with L.A. County Fire and traffic
calming devices. Director Rigg said they’ve always engaged the Fire Department in the discussion of
traffic calming devices because they know there is a concern about response times. In the past, the Fire
Department has opposed all the speed humps we have in the City and expressed their concerns, as they
did with the speed cushions. The Traffic Safety Committee is trying to balance overall safety as well
as a variety of other factors. The Fire Department feels speed humps or cushions may slow down a fire
truck or ambulance, but hopefully they have a lot less to respond to because there are less accidents.
He said they’ve taken their input in the past, weighed it, and the Traffic Safety Committee has installed
a number of devices. As of January 1st, the Fire Department changed their Code (Title 32) and it has a
specific prohibition against traffic calming measures, unless specifically authorized by them. As a
matter of Code, there is a prohibition of installing additional [traffic calming measures] in the future,
unless they’ve approved them. He said in his conversations with them, being that we are in a very high
fire hazard severity zone, they would oppose anything. If we were to go forward, we would need to
make sure to get their approval with any additional speed humps or cushions in the future, or to
evaluate it further as a matter of law and decide that we actually can do it.

Public Works Director Rigg said per Council direction, staff investigated the structural adequacy of

in 1992 when we had a seismic evaluation of the building and retrofits, and what was done today.

called ‘immediate occupancy’, or that the building is operable after the earthquake so we can still set
up our Emergency Response Center and this building will still be occupiable. When the seismic
analysis was done in 1992, it was done to a life safety performance level (the building can fail, but
people need to be able to get out safety), which is why there is a difference in their analysis and why

estimate provided, except for interior finishes and nonstructural elements. These are invasive types of

which staff estimates will cost ~$50,000. He said they could either implement the different items
